_2024_1_SCR_623.case_name: Mariam Fasihuddin & Anr. v. State by Adugodi Police Station & Anr.

Discussed in context of 'forgery' requiring a fabricated document with intent to cheat.
Examined for fraudulent use of documents as genuine.

_2024_1_SCR_623.abstract_facts: The case involves allegations against the appellants of forgery related to obtaining a passport for a minor child. The appellants claim the actions were in line with instructions, but it is alleged that the signatures on the passport application were forged. The case arose amidst personal disputes between the appellants and the respondent husband, leading to competing legal actions.

propositions.text: For the offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC, fraudulent and dishonest intention must exist from the inception when the promise or representation was made.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The fundamental elements of 'deceit' and 'damage or injury' are requisite for constituting the offence of cheating under Section 420 IPC.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: To establish the offence of forgery, the accused must have fabricated an instrument with the intention that it would be used for the purpose of cheating.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: 'Further investigation' under Section 173(8) CrPC requires obtaining new evidence and not merely reassessing existing material.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Under Section 12(b) of the Passports Act, an individual must knowingly furnish false information or suppress material information to be found guilty.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

defense.analysis: Quashing precedent establishing that dishonest intention at inception is mandatory for Section 420, directly supporting lack of prima facie criminality for bail.
use_for: Argue absence of dishonest or fraudulent intention at inception, which is an indispensable ingredient for Section 420 IPC
Establish that essential ingredients of forgery under Sections 468/471 are not satisfied prima facie (flagged as quashing precedent applicable to bail prima facie threshold)
against: The prosecution may rely on the fact that this case arose from specific allegations of forged signatures and still required close scrutiny, so the court may say a similar forgery allegation warrants investigation before bail.
distinguish: This precedent was decided on the merits of criminal liability in a passport-related dispute, not on anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC/BNSS 482, so its direct bail value is limited.

_2023_10_SCR_411.case_name: Pratibha Manchanda & Anr. v. State of Haryana & Anr.

matched_statutes.note: Anticipatory bail aims to safeguard individual rights while balancing public interest and ensuring a fair investigation.

_2023_10_SCR_411.abstract_facts: The appellants, alleging ownership of a land parcel in Gurugram, claimed never to have sold it or executed any power of attorney. They discovered that mutations were sought based on a purportedly forged sale deed and power of attorney from 1996. An FIR was lodged against the accused, who sought anticipatory bail from the High Court. The High Court granted bail, but the Supreme Court set aside the bail considering the need for custodial interrogation.

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail is designed to safeguard individual rights and prevent harassment from arrest, while balancing against public interest and ensuring the gravity of the offence is considered.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The custody of suspects is justified to ensure fair and thorough investigation when there are allegations of forgery and misappropriation of property.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The original GPA's absence raises doubts about the legitimacy of transactions claimed by the accused and underscores the need for investigation.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: In cases of alleged land fraud, thorough investigation by authorities is necessary, and anticipatory bail complicates uncovering the truth.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Bail cancellation should occur only with substantial reasons, but correcting an erroneous bail order differs.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

prosecution.analysis: Directly supports prosecution: land fraud involving forged deeds warrants denial of anticipatory bail, and civil remedy is no bar.
use_for: Oppose anticipatory bail in fraudulent land conveyance involving forged documents and impersonation
Argue that pendency of civil proceedings or availability of civil remedy is no bar to criminal prosecution for land fraud
against: The defence may rely on the general bail principle that anticipatory bail balances individual liberty against public interest and is not to be denied mechanically.
distinguish: The precedent specifically arose from a land fraud involving a purportedly forged sale deed and GPA; if the defence emphasizes a different factual matrix, prosecution can still rely on the case because the input case also involves forgery-related offences under IPC 465, 468, 471 and cheating under IPC 420.

_2023_5_SCC_360.case_name: Sarabjit Kaur v. State of Punjab & Anr.
_2023_5_SCC_360.disposition: Appeal allowed. FIR No. 248 of 2017 under Section 420 IPC and consequential proceedings quashed.

matched_statutes.note: Cheating in property sale agreement dispute

_2023_5_SCC_360.abstract_facts: The appellant entered into an agreement to sell a plot of land and received earnest money. The sale deed could not be executed because an NOC was not obtained from local development authorities. The purchaser filed an FIR under Section 420 IPC alleging cheating. The Supreme Court held that mere failure to perform a contractual promise or execute a sale deed gives rise to a civil remedy for breach of contract, and does not constitute criminal cheating under Section 420 IPC unless dishonest intention existed at the inception of the contract.

propositions.text: A breach of contract or failure to execute a sale deed does not give rise to criminal prosecution under Section 420 IPC unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown to have existed at the inception of the transaction.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Courts must prevent the abuse of criminal process where parties seek to short-circuit civil remedies for recovery of money or specific performance of land agreements by filing criminal complaints of cheating.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

prosecution.analysis: This is a quashing case, not an anticipatory bail decision, so it does not directly govern custody/bail; however, it is useful to the prosecution only by contrast, because it draws the civil-criminal boundary in property transactions and requires scrutiny of dishonest intention at inception. The prosecution can distinguish it by emphasizing that the present case also invokes forged documents and use of forged documents (Sections 465/468/471/423), which go beyond a mere failure to perform an agreement to sell.
use_for: To argue that where dishonest intention at inception is shown through forged documents and deceptive inducement, the dispute is not a mere civil breach and criminal process is warranted.

To contend that the present case should not be treated as a simple land/title dispute because the allegations include forgery and use of forged documents, supporting prima facie criminality and custodial interrogation.
against: The accused may rely on the decision to argue that if the matter is only a failed property transaction without proof of initial dishonest intent, criminal proceedings should not be used to settle a civil dispute.
distinguish: Here, unlike a bare agreement-to-sell dispute, the invoked sections include forgery, use of forged documents, and false execution of deed, which materially expands the allegation beyond mere non-performance.

The precedent arose in a quashing context under Section 420 alone, whereas the present matter is anticipatory bail with multiple forgery-related sections and a prosecution claim of need for custodial interrogation.

defense.analysis: This decision supports the defense by reaffirming that criminal cheating cannot be inferred from a mere failure to complete a property transaction unless dishonest intention existed at the inception. In anticipatory bail, it helps argue that the FIR reflects a civil land dispute being converted into a criminal case to exert pressure, weakening the need for custodial arrest.
use_for: Argue that allegations under Sections 420/417 do not by themselves establish criminality where the dispute arises from a land transaction and the prosecution has not shown dishonest intention at the inception.
Contend that the complaint is an attempt to bypass civil remedies and use criminal process as leverage, which supports protection of personal liberty at the anticipatory bail stage.
against: The precedent is a quashing case, not an anticipatory bail decision, so the State may argue it only addresses maintainability of criminal prosecution and does not by itself mandate bail.
distinguish: Unlike a pure breach-of-contract scenario, the present case also invokes forgery-related sections (IPC 465, 468, 471, 423), so the defense must still separately contest the alleged false document/forgery ingredients.

_2018_7_SCC_581.case_name: Sheila Sebastian v. R. Jawaharaj & Anr.
_2018_7_SCC_581.disposition: Appeals dismissed; acquittal of accused under Sections 465, 468, 471 IPC confirmed.

matched_statutes.note: Definition and basic ingredients of forgery
Forgery for the purpose of cheating
Using forged document as genuine

_2018_7_SCC_581.abstract_facts: The appellant filed a private complaint alleging that the respondent, an advocate, created a forged Power of Attorney (GPA) in the name of the appellant's deceased father and attempted to transfer property. The Supreme Court examined the legal requirements for establishing the offence of forgery under Sections 463, 464, and 468 IPC, specifically holding that a charge of forgery cannot stand unless the accused is established to be the maker or author of the false document.

propositions.text: Making of a false document under Section 464 IPC is the sine qua non for the offence of forgery under Section 463 and Section 468 IPC. Unless the prosecution establishes that the accused himself made or created the false document, a charge of forgery cannot be sustained.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Suspicion, however grave, cannot take the place of proof in criminal law; in allegations of forged property documents, the essential statutory ingredients under Sections 464 and 465 must be strictly established.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

prosecution.analysis: This authority is adverse to the prosecution because it reiterates that forgery under Sections 465/468/471 IPC requires proof that the accused made or caused the false document to be made, and that suspicion cannot replace proof. In anticipatory bail, the defence may use it to argue that mere allegation of forged documents is insufficient unless the prosecution can show the applicant's direct role in creation of the forged instrument.
use_for: Not useful for opposing bail; it tends to dilute the prosecution case unless the prosecution can specifically connect the applicant to making or causing the false document
If the prosecution has evidence of authorship/execution/causation, this case helps frame the precise issue that must still be met before invoking forgery-related offences
against: The defence will rely on this case to argue that, without proof that the applicant made or caused the forged document, Sections 465/468/471 are not made out prima facie
distinguish: This precedent arose at the quashing/acquittal stage, not anticipatory bail, so the prosecution needs only a prima facie case and need for custodial interrogation rather than proof beyond reasonable doubt

The present case also includes cheating-related provisions (Sections 420, 417, 423 IPC), so even if authorship of the forged document is contested, fraudulent inducement and dishonest execution may still independently sustain opposition to bail

defense.analysis: This authority strongly helps the defense on the merits of the alleged forgery/cheating sections because it reiterates that making of a false document under Section 464 is the sine qua non for Sections 465/468, and suspicion cannot substitute for proof. In anticipatory bail, it supports the argument that the allegations are legally weak at the threshold and therefore liberty should not be curtailed on a bare assertion of forgery.
use_for: Argue that unless the prosecution can show the accused himself made, signed, executed, or caused the false document to be made, the forgery allegations under Sections 465/468 are prima facie incomplete.

Submit that the case rests only on suspicion or disputed documentary assertions, so criminal process should not be used to deny anticipatory bail where the foundational ingredient of false document is not clearly made out.
against: The prosecution may argue that this is a quashing/acquittal decision on merits, not a bail ruling, so it does not by itself mandate anticipatory bail.
distinguish: The precedent arose in a quashing context rather than anticipatory bail, so its direct procedural force is limited; however, the substantive holding on Section 464 remains highly useful to show weak prima facie criminality.

_2025_9_SCR_982.case_name: Anna Waman Bhalerao v. State of Maharashtra
_2025_9_SCR_982.abstract_facts: The case concerns anticipatory bail applications filed by appellants, former government officials, following allegations of facilitating fraudulent property mutations based on forged documents during their tenure. The events occurred between 1996-1998, but the FIR was not filed until 2019. Attempts for anticipatory bail were made at both session and High Court levels, with interim protection granted intermittently. The Supreme Court was approached after the High Court's final rejection of anticipatory bail, amid concerns of inordinate delays in the case.

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail applications should be disposed of expeditiously, preferably within two months, except when delays are caused by the parties.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: In matters concerning personal liberty, bail courts must be sensitive and ensure constitutional ethos is upheld; prolonged delays in bail decisions are a denial of justice.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Custodial interrogation may be essential even in cases based largely on documentary evidence, to trace transactions and ascertain complicity.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The rejection of anticipatory bail by a High Court can be affirmed on appeal if interim protections were already extensively enjoyed without investigation cooperation.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

prosecution.analysis: This Supreme Court anticipatory bail decision directly assists the prosecution on the need for custodial interrogation in a document-based forgery/cheating case, especially where the alleged acts involve fraudulent mutations and forged documents. It also supports the argument that prior interim protection and non-cooperation can justify continued refusal of pre-arrest bail.
use_for: Argue that even in predominantly documentary offences under Sections 420, 465, 468 and 471 IPC, custodial interrogation may be necessary to trace the chain of transactions, identify the origin/use of forged documents, and ascertain the accused's role.

Support rejection of anticipatory bail where the accused had already enjoyed interim protection and the investigation was not meaningfully advanced, indicating that pre-arrest liberty may frustrate effective inquiry.
against: The decision also reiterates that anticipatory bail matters must be decided expeditiously and that prolonged delay in bail adjudication is disapproved, which the defence may invoke to seek protection.
distinguish: The precedent involved alleged fraudulent property mutations by former government officials, whereas the present case is assessed on the cited IPC forgery/cheating provisions without those specific administrative mutation facts; however, both involve forged documents and alleged deception.

_2009_8_SCC_751.disposition: Appeals allowed. Order taking cognizance under Sections 420, 467, 471 IPC quashed.

_2009_8_SCC_751.abstract_facts: The first appellant executed two registered sale deeds in favor of second and third appellants in respect of a parcel of land. The complainant alleged that the land belonged to him and that the first appellant, having no title, executed fraudulent sale deeds asserting ownership. A complaint was filed for offences under Sections 420, 467, 471, and 504 IPC. The Supreme Court examined whether executing a sale deed conveying property not belonging to the executant constitutes making a false document under Section 464 IPC, cheating under Section 420 IPC, or forgery under Sections 467/471 IPC.

propositions.text: When a person executes a document conveying property asserting that he is the owner thereof, knowing that he is not, he does not make a false document under Section 464 IPC, as he does not impersonate another or sign in another's name. Selling property one does not own does not constitute forgery.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Unless a false document is made as defined under Section 464 IPC, offences of forgery under Section 463 and aggravated forgery under Sections 467 and 471 IPC cannot be sustained.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Where a dispute is fundamentally a civil dispute over title to immovable property, the complainant cannot invoke the criminal process under Section 420 IPC to exert pressure on the accused.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

prosecution.analysis: Adverse defense authority holding sale without title is not forgery under Section 464; prosecution must distinguish by proving actual document fabrication.
use_for: Anticipate and neutralize the defence reliance on this case by stressing that it is a quashing decision on a land-title dispute, not a bail-order approving release in a case with alleged forged documents and use of forged documents.

Argue that, despite the defence's likely reliance, the present case involves allegations under Sections 465, 468, 471, 420, 417, and 423 IPC and therefore the prosecution must emphasize the specific acts of forgery/forged use and inducement that take the matter beyond a bare title dispute.
against: The accused may rely on p1-p3 to contend that at most this is a civil dispute over land and that mere execution of a deed without title does not amount to forgery or cheating.
distinguish: Distinguishable if the accused fabricated false ownership documents or impersonated the true owner, which falls squarely within Section 464

defense.analysis: Primary defense authority: executing a deed conveying land without title does not constitute a false document under Section 464, negating Sections 467/468/471.
use_for: Decisive landmark holding: Executing a sale deed conveying property not owned does NOT constitute 'making a false document' under Section 464 IPC
In the absence of a 'false document' under Section 464, charges under Sections 467, 468, and 471 IPC cannot stand
Civil dispute over ownership/title to agricultural land cannot be converted into criminal offences of cheating and forgery
against: The prosecution may argue that this case arose at the quashing stage, so it decides merits of cognizance rather than the separate discretion involved in anticipatory bail.
distinguish: The present matter is at the anticipatory bail stage, not quashing, so the defense can rely on the legal principle while acknowledging that the court is only assessing prima facie liberty interests and not finally adjudicating guilt.

_1980_3_SCR_383.case_name: GURBAKSH SINGH SIBBIA ETC. v. STATE OF PUNJAB

matched_statutes.note: Section 438(1) empowers High Courts and Sessions Courts to grant anticipatory bail based on reasonable belief of arrest for a non-bailable offense. Conditions from Section 437 are not automatically applicable.

_1980_3_SCR_383.abstract_facts: The case involves allegations against a former Minister of Irrigation and Power in the Punjab government, accused of political corruption. Anticipatory bail applications were filed in the High Court, which were then referred to a Full Bench. The High Court imposed several constraints on the grant of anticipatory bail, emphasizing it should be rarely used. The appeals reached the Supreme Court to address the balance between individual liberty and investigational powers of the police under Section 438 of CrPC 1973.

propositions.text: The High Court and Court of Session have discretionary power to grant anticipatory bail based on facts and circumstances of each case.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail should not generally be granted as a blanket order that covers all potential offences.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: An application for anticipatory bail cannot be based on vague or general apprehensions of arrest.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail cannot be granted after the arrest of the accused.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Section 438 of the CrPC provides a procedure focused on protecting personal liberty before arrest.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The limitations of Section 437 are not automatically applicable to Section 438.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail can be granted even if the FIR is not filed yet, as long as there is a reasonable belief of arrest.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Conditions can be imposed while granting anticipatory bail to ensure cooperation with the police and no tampering with evidence.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Section 438 is not an unconstitutional provision as it ensures fairness in its procedural safeguards for anticipatory bail.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: A higher court should not impose overly restrictive conditions not found in Section 438, as it leaves room for judicial discretion.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

defense.analysis: This is a foundational anticipatory bail authority directly supporting the defense on the Section 438/Article 21 liberty framework, discretion of the court, and the availability of protective conditions. It does not address the merits of forgery/cheating allegations, so its value is principled rather than fact-specific.
use_for: Argue that anticipatory bail exists to protect personal liberty before arrest and should be considered on the facts of each case, not denied mechanically.
Show willingness to accept reasonable conditions to secure cooperation with investigation, while resisting a blanket denial of pre-arrest protection.
against: The prosecution may rely on the same case to seek restrictive conditions, stress the need to avoid tampering with evidence, and argue that vague or general apprehensions are insufficient.
distinguish: The precedent concerns the general scope of Section 438 and not the substantive ingredients of IPC Sections 465, 468, 471, 420, 417, or 423; it therefore does not decide whether the present forgery/cheating allegations are made out.

defense_precedents.case_name: GURBAKSH SINGH SIBBIA ETC. v. STATE OF PUNJAB

matched_statutes.note: Section 438(1) empowers High Courts and Sessions Courts to grant anticipatory bail based on reasonable belief of arrest for a non-bailable offense. Conditions from Section 437 are not automatically applicable.

defense_precedents.abstract_facts: The case involves allegations against a former Minister of Irrigation and Power in the Punjab government, accused of political corruption. Anticipatory bail applications were filed in the High Court, which were then referred to a Full Bench. The High Court imposed several constraints on the grant of anticipatory bail, emphasizing it should be rarely used. The appeals reached the Supreme Court to address the balance between individual liberty and investigational powers of the police under Section 438 of CrPC 1973.

propositions.text: The High Court and Court of Session have discretionary power to grant anticipatory bail based on facts and circumstances of each case.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail should not generally be granted as a blanket order that covers all potential offences.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: An application for anticipatory bail cannot be based on vague or general apprehensions of arrest.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail cannot be granted after the arrest of the accused.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Section 438 of the CrPC provides a procedure focused on protecting personal liberty before arrest.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: The limitations of Section 437 are not automatically applicable to Section 438.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Anticipatory bail can be granted even if the FIR is not filed yet, as long as there is a reasonable belief of arrest.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Conditions can be imposed while granting anticipatory bail to ensure cooperation with the police and no tampering with evidence.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: Section 438 is not an unconstitutional provision as it ensures fairness in its procedural safeguards for anticipatory bail.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

propositions.text: A higher court should not impose overly restrictive conditions not found in Section 438, as it leaves room for judicial discretion.
propositions.speaker: supreme_court

against_role: The decision also reiterates that anticipatory bail matters must be decided expeditiously and that prolonged delay in bail adjudication is disapproved, which the defence may invoke to seek protection.
